People Who Never Reached Age 58

Mustafa Kemal Atatürk

Birth date: May 18, 1881

Death date: November 9, 1938

Age: 57

Mustafa Kemal Atatürk was the Ottoman-born soldier, statesman, and reformer who founded the Republic of Turkey and served as its first president from 1923 to 1938. A commander at Gallipoli and leader of the Turkish War of Independence, he reshaped the new republic through secular, legal, educational, linguistic, and cultural reforms. In his final year his health declined from liver disease, commonly identified as cirrhosis; he died at Dolmabahçe Palace in Istanbul on 10 November 1938, aged 57.

L. L. Zamenhof

Birth date: December 14, 1859

Death date: April 13, 1917

Age: 57

L. L. Zamenhof, born Ludwik Lejzer Zamenhof, was a Polish-Jewish physician and ophthalmologist best remembered as the creator of Esperanto, the international auxiliary language he introduced in 1887 under the hopeful pseudonym Dr. Esperanto. Inspired by the conflicts of multilingual Białystok, he imagined language as a practical bridge between peoples. He died in Warsaw on 14 April 1917 at age 57, reportedly of heart failure, and was buried in the Jewish cemetery on Okopowa Street.

Warren G. Harding

Birth date: November 1, 1865

Death date: August 1, 1923

Age: 57

Warren G. Harding was the 29th president of the United States, a Republican from Ohio who rose from newspaper publisher to state senator, lieutenant governor, U.S. senator, and president. His 1920 campaign promised a “return to normalcy” after World War I, and he was popular during his lifetime, though scandals later damaged his reputation. In 1923, while traveling through the western United States, he became ill and died suddenly in San Francisco, most likely from a heart attack, at age 57.

Adolf Hitler

Birth date: April 19, 1889

Death date: April 29, 1945

Age: 56
Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Extremely controversial because he was the Nazi dictator whose regime initiated the Second World War in Europe and carried out the Holocaust and other mass murders, persecutions, and aggressive wars.

Adolf Hitler was an Austrian-born German politician, leader of the Nazi Party, and dictator of Germany from 1933 to 1945. His regime launched the Second World War in Europe and was central to the Holocaust, the genocide of about six million Jews and millions of other victims. In April 1945, with Berlin surrounded by Soviet forces and Nazi Germany collapsing, Hitler withdrew into the Führerbunker and died by suicide on 30 April 1945, aged 56.

William Shakespeare

Birth date: April 22, 1564

Death date: April 22, 1616

Age: 52

William Shakespeare was an English playwright, poet, and actor from Stratford-upon-Avon, celebrated as the leading dramatist of the English language. His plays, sonnets, and narrative poems shaped world literature and theatre for centuries. He died in Stratford on 23 April 1616, traditionally his 52nd birthday; the precise cause of death is not known, though he was buried two days later at Holy Trinity Church.

Michael Jackson

Birth date: August 28, 1958

Death date: June 24, 2009

Age: 50
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Michael Jackson is highly controversial because of repeated allegations of child sexual abuse, major criminal and civil proceedings, and later documentary accounts that kept public debate active after his death. He was acquitted in his 2005 criminal trial and denied the allegations, so the controversy includes both serious accusations and disputed legal/public interpretations.

Michael Jackson was an American singer, songwriter, dancer, and global pop icon whose music, videos, choreography, and style reshaped popular entertainment. From his childhood with the Jackson 5 to solo milestones such as Off the Wall, Thriller, Bad, and Dangerous, he became one of the best-selling and most influential performers in history. He died in Los Angeles on June 25, 2009, at age 50, from cardiac arrest linked to acute propofol and sedative intoxication while preparing for his This Is It concert series.

Abraham Lincoln

Birth date: February 11, 1809

Death date: April 14, 1865

Age: 56

Abraham Lincoln was the 16th president of the United States, a self-educated lawyer and Republican leader who guided the Union through the Civil War and became central to the abolition of slavery. He was shot by John Wilkes Booth at Ford’s Theatre on April 14, 1865, and died the next morning in Washington, D.C.

Vladimir Lenin

Birth date: April 21, 1870

Death date: January 20, 1924

Age: 53
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Lenin is highly controversial because he founded and led a one-party revolutionary state, used political repression against opponents, and is associated with the Red Terror, civil-war coercion, censorship, and the creation of institutions that shaped later Soviet authoritarianism.

Vladimir Lenin, born Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov, was a Russian revolutionary, Marxist theorist, founder of the Bolshevik faction, and the first head of government of Soviet Russia and later the Soviet Union. He led the October Revolution of 1917 and shaped the one-party Soviet state through policies including nationalization, civil-war centralization, and the New Economic Policy. After a series of debilitating strokes in 1922 and 1923, Lenin’s health collapsed; he died at Gorki on 21 January 1924 at the age of 53.

Julius Caesar

Birth date: July 11, 100 BCE

Death date: March 14, 44 BCE

Age: 55
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Julius Caesar is controversial as a conqueror and authoritarian political leader. His campaigns in Gaul caused mass death, enslavement, and displacement, and his crossing of the Rubicon, civil war, and dictatorship helped destroy the Roman Republic.

Julius Caesar was a Roman general, statesman and author whose conquest of Gaul, alliance with Pompey and Crassus, victory in civil war and dictatorship reshaped the Roman Republic and helped prepare the Roman Empire. After accepting the title dictator for life in 44 BC, he was stabbed to death by a senatorial conspiracy led by Brutus and Cassius on the Ides of March, an assassination that triggered another round of civil wars.

Ludwig van Beethoven

Birth date: December 15, 1770

Death date: March 25, 1827

Age: 56

Ludwig van Beethoven was a German composer and pianist whose music helped drive the transition from the Classical era to Romanticism. Born in Bonn and later based in Vienna, he transformed the symphony, sonata, concerto, and string quartet, creating works such as the Fifth and Ninth Symphonies, Fidelio, the late piano sonatas, and the late quartets. His growing deafness made his career even more extraordinary. After several months of serious illness marked by symptoms such as jaundice, swelling, and abdominal fluid, he died in Vienna on 26 March 1827 at the age of 56.

Dante Alighieri

Birth date: May 31, 1265

Death date: September 13, 1321

Age: 56

Dante Alighieri was a Florentine poet, political exile, philosopher, and author of the Divine Comedy, one of the defining works of world literature and a cornerstone of the Italian language. Banished from Florence in 1302, he spent his later life moving between Italian courts and completed his masterpiece in exile. He died in Ravenna in September 1321, aged 56, most likely from malaria contracted after returning from a diplomatic mission to Venice.

Napoleon

Birth date: August 14, 1769

Death date: May 4, 1821

Age: 51
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Napoleon is highly controversial because his rule combined major legal and administrative reforms with authoritarian government, censorship, dynastic ambition, and years of large-scale war across Europe. His 1802 restoration of slavery in French colonies and the violent campaigns of the Napoleonic era are central reasons his legacy is disputed.

Napoleon Bonaparte, later Napoleon I, was a Corsican-born French general and statesman who rose during the French Revolution and became Emperor of the French. He reshaped Europe through military campaigns, state reforms, and the Napoleonic Code, leaving a legacy admired for administrative modernization and criticized for war, authoritarian rule, and the restoration of slavery in French colonies. After his defeat at Waterloo, he was exiled to Saint Helena, where his health declined. He died at Longwood House on 5 May 1821, aged 51, most commonly attributed to stomach cancer.

Friedrich Nietzsche

Birth date: October 14, 1844

Death date: August 24, 1900

Age: 55

Friedrich Wilhelm Nietzsche was a German philosopher, classical philologist, poet, and cultural critic whose work reshaped modern thought through ideas such as perspectivism, the critique of morality, the death of God, eternal recurrence, and the Übermensch. A former professor at Basel, he became an independent writer after years of illness. In 1889 he suffered a severe mental collapse and spent his final years incapacitated under family care. After strokes and pneumonia in 1900, he died in Weimar at the age of 55.

René Descartes

Birth date: March 30, 1596

Death date: February 10, 1650

Age: 53

René Descartes was a French philosopher, mathematician, and scientist whose method of radical doubt and famous idea “I think, therefore I am” helped shape modern philosophy. He also linked algebra and geometry, giving his name to Cartesian coordinates. In 1649 he moved to Stockholm to tutor Queen Christina of Sweden; the cold climate, early-morning lessons, and illness are traditionally connected with the pneumonia that led to his death on 11 February 1650, at age 53.

Christopher Columbus

Birth date: October 30, 1451

Death date: May 19, 1506

Age: 54
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Christopher Columbus is highly controversial because his voyages are tied to European colonization of the Americas, Indigenous dispossession, forced labor, enslavement, violence, and catastrophic population loss. He is also criticized for his conduct as governor in the Caribbean and for becoming a symbol in modern debates over conquest and colonial memory.

Christopher Columbus was a Genoese navigator and explorer whose four Spanish-sponsored Atlantic voyages transformed European knowledge of the Americas and helped launch a long era of exploration, conquest, and colonization. Ambitious, skilled, and controversial, he sought a westward route to Asia but reached Caribbean lands instead. After years of illness, disputes over titles and revenues, and declining royal favor, he died in Valladolid, Spain, on 20 May 1506, still convinced he had reached the fringes of Asia. He was 54.

Death date: October 4, 2011

Age: 56

Steve Jobs was an American entrepreneur, inventor, and investor who co-founded Apple, helped shape the personal-computer revolution, built NeXT, and played a major role in Pixar’s rise. Known for his intense product vision, he helped bring the Macintosh, iPod, iPhone, and iPad into popular culture. He died at his home in Palo Alto on October 5, 2011, from complications related to a previously treated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, after years of serious health problems.

Virgil, born Publius Vergilius Maro, was the great Roman poet of the Augustan age and the author of the Eclogues, the Georgics, and the Aeneid, the epic that became a cornerstone of Latin literature. In 19 BC, after meeting Augustus in Athens and traveling in Greece, he fell ill, returned to Italy, and died at Brundisium before finishing the Aeneid; Augustus ordered the poem preserved rather than burned.

John F. Kennedy was the 35th president of the United States, a former U.S. Navy officer, congressman, and senator from Massachusetts whose presidency became closely associated with Cold War crises, the Peace Corps, the space race, and a youthful vision of public service. He was assassinated in Dallas, Texas, on November 22, 1963, while riding in a presidential motorcade, and was pronounced dead shortly afterward at age 46.

Death date: February 16, 1673

Age: 51

Molière, born Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, was the towering comic playwright, actor, and theatre director of 17th-century France, famous for Tartuffe, The Misanthrope, The School for Wives, and The Imaginary Invalid. His sharp satire of hypocrisy, pretension, medicine, marriage, and social vanity made him a central figure in French literature. Already weakened by illness, he collapsed after performing as Argan in The Imaginary Invalid and died in Paris a few hours later, aged 51.

Albrecht Dürer

Birth date: May 20, 1471

Death date: April 5, 1528

Age: 56

Albrecht Dürer was the defining artist of the German Renaissance: a painter, engraver, printmaker, and theorist whose woodcuts, engravings, portraits, and studies of proportion carried his reputation across Europe. He worked from Nuremberg, travelled to Italy and the Low Countries, and became admired by artists and patrons far beyond Germany. After returning from the Netherlands in 1521, he suffered years of failing health and produced less art while focusing on theoretical writings. He died in Nuremberg on 6 April 1528, aged 56, and was buried in the Johannisfriedhof cemetery.

Death date: July 14, 1904

Age: 44

Anton Pavlovich Chekhov was a Russian playwright, short-story writer, and physician whose spare, psychologically subtle style helped reshape modern drama and fiction. His major plays include The Seagull, Uncle Vanya, Three Sisters, and The Cherry Orchard, while his stories remain landmarks of literary realism. Long ill with tuberculosis, he traveled to Badenweiler, Germany, seeking relief; he died there on 15 July 1904 at the age of 44 after years of declining health.

Birth date: July 15, 1872

Death date: June 17, 1928

Age: 55

Roald Amundsen was a Norwegian polar explorer and one of the defining figures of the Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration. He led the first successful expedition through the Northwest Passage and, in 1911, became the first person to reach the South Pole. In June 1928, he disappeared in the Arctic while flying a rescue mission for the crashed Italia airship; wreckage was later found, but his body was never recovered.

Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky

Birth date: May 6, 1840

Death date: November 5, 1893

Age: 53

Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky was a Russian Romantic-era composer whose vivid melodies and dramatic orchestration made works such as Swan Lake, The Sleeping Beauty, The Nutcracker, the 1812 Overture, Eugene Onegin, and the Pathétique Symphony central to the classical repertoire. He brought Russian music to an international audience while blending Western conservatory technique with a deeply personal expressive style. He died in Saint Petersburg on 6 November 1893, aged 53. His death is traditionally attributed to cholera and its complications, though later speculation about suicide has remained controversial and is not supported by firm documentary evidence.

Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter whose bold colour, expressive brushwork and emotional intensity helped shape modern art. Although he worked seriously as an artist for only about a decade, he produced masterpieces including Sunflowers, The Starry Night and many self-portraits. He struggled with mental illness and poverty, and died in Auvers-sur-Oise after shooting himself, passing away two days later at the age of 37.

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was an Austrian composer and musician of the Classical period, celebrated for operas, symphonies, concertos, chamber music, and sacred works that helped define Western music. A child prodigy from Salzburg, he later built his mature career in Vienna. He died there on 5 December 1791 at age 35 after a short illness; the exact medical cause remains uncertain, and his Requiem was left unfinished.

Thomas Aquinas was an Italian Dominican friar, theologian, philosopher, and one of the defining minds of medieval Scholasticism. He joined Aristotelian philosophy with Christian theology, shaped Catholic intellectual tradition, and wrote major works including the Summa Theologiae and Summa contra Gentiles. In 1274, while traveling to the Second Council of Lyon, he became seriously ill after a head injury and was taken to Fossanova Abbey, where Cistercian monks cared for him until his death on 7 March.

Death date: November 29, 1900

Age: 46

Oscar Wilde was an Irish author, poet, essayist and playwright, celebrated for his dazzling wit, aesthetic style and works such as The Picture of Dorian Gray and The Importance of Being Earnest. A defining literary figure of late Victorian culture, he became famous in London for his comedies, epigrams and flamboyant public persona. After imprisonment and exile, his health declined; he died in Paris on 30 November 1900 from meningitis, commonly linked to an ear infection, at the age of 46.

Matsuo Bashō

Birth date: December 31, 1644

Death date: November 27, 1694

Age: 50

Matsuo Bashō was the great Edo-period Japanese poet who transformed haikai and later became celebrated as the supreme master of haiku. Born near Ueno in Iga Province, he built a life around teaching, travel, literary experiment, and sharply observed scenes of nature and impermanence. His travel writing, especially the journey associated with The Narrow Road to the Deep North, helped make wandering itself part of his artistic legend. In 1694, while traveling again, Bashō fell ill in Osaka, apparently from a stomach ailment, and died there on November 28 at about age 50, surrounded by the aura of the road that had shaped his poetry.

Max Weber

Birth date: April 20, 1864

Death date: June 13, 1920

Age: 56

Max Weber was a German sociologist, historian, jurist, and political economist whose work helped shape modern sociology and social theory. He is especially remembered for The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, his analysis of bureaucracy, authority, rationalization, and the role of ideas in economic life. After the First World War, he advised on Germany’s new constitutional order and returned to teaching in Munich. He died there on 14 June 1920 at age 56, from pneumonia often linked to the influenza pandemic, leaving major work unfinished.

Martin Luther King Jr.

Birth date: January 14, 1929

Death date: April 3, 1968

Age: 39

Martin Luther King Jr. was an American Baptist minister and civil rights leader whose advocacy of nonviolent resistance made him one of the defining figures of the U.S. civil rights movement. He helped lead the Montgomery bus boycott, co-founded the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, delivered the landmark “I Have a Dream” speech, and received the 1964 Nobel Peace Prize. In his final years, he broadened his work to address poverty and opposition to the Vietnam War. King was assassinated on April 4, 1968, in Memphis, Tennessee, while supporting striking sanitation workers and preparing the Poor People’s Campaign. He died at the age of 39.

George Orwell

Birth date: June 24, 1903

Death date: January 20, 1950

Age: 46

George Orwell, born Eric Arthur Blair, was an English novelist, essayist, journalist, and critic whose clear prose and fierce opposition to totalitarianism made him one of the defining political writers of the twentieth century. He is best remembered for Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four, works that turned terms like Big Brother and Orwellian into lasting cultural shorthand. His final years were marked by severe tuberculosis; after completing Nineteen Eighty-Four, he was treated in hospital in London, where he died from the disease on 21 January 1950 at the age of 46.

Franz Kafka

Birth date: July 2, 1883

Death date: June 2, 1924

Age: 40

Franz Kafka was a Prague-born German-language Jewish writer whose fiction transformed modern literature with visions of alienation, absurd bureaucracy, guilt, anxiety, and fragile identity. His best-known works include The Metamorphosis, The Trial, and The Castle, many of which became famous only after his friend Max Brod ignored Kafka’s request to destroy unpublished manuscripts. He died in 1924 at a sanatorium near Vienna after tuberculosis, especially affecting his throat, made eating extremely painful; he was 40 years old.

Horace

Birth date: December 7, 65 BCE

Death date: November 26, 8 BCE

Age: 56

Horace, born Quintus Horatius Flaccus, was one of ancient Rome’s great lyric poets, admired for the Odes, Satires, Epistles, and Ars Poetica. From modest origins in Venusia, he studied in Rome and Athens, fought on the losing republican side at Philippi, then rebuilt his life as a poet under the patronage of Maecenas in the age of Augustus. He died in Rome on 27 November 8 BC, reportedly after a sudden illness, only days before his 57th birthday, and was buried near Maecenas.

Qin Shi Huang

Birth date: January 31, 259 BCE

Death date: July 11, 210 BCE

Age: 49
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Qin Shi Huang was an authoritarian imperial ruler whose legacy includes wars of conquest, harsh Legalist punishments, forced labor on enormous state projects, censorship, and traditional accounts of book burning and executions of scholars. Some details of those accounts are debated, but his rule is strongly associated with coercive centralized power.

Qin Shi Huang, born Ying Zheng, was the founder of the Qin dynasty and the first emperor of a unified China. After defeating the rival Warring States, he centralized rule, standardized writing, weights, measures and coinage, expanded roads and walls, and left behind the famous mausoleum guarded by the Terracotta Army. He died in 210 BC during his fifth inspection tour of eastern China after becoming seriously ill; later tradition links his final years to an obsession with immortality, and mercury-based elixirs have often been suggested as a possible factor, though the exact cause remains uncertain.

Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Osama bin Laden is extremely controversial as the founder and leader of al-Qaeda, the terrorist organization responsible for mass-casualty attacks including September 11, 2001. His ideology, planning, and public justification of violence against civilians make him one of the most notorious extremist figures of the modern era.

Osama bin Laden was a Saudi-born militant leader and the founder of al-Qaeda, the extremist organization behind major terrorist attacks including the September 11 attacks in the United States. Born into a wealthy Saudi family, he became involved in jihadist networks during the Soviet-Afghan War and later built al-Qaeda into an international terrorist movement. He died at age 54 on 2 May 2011, when U.S. Navy SEALs killed him during a raid on his compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan.

Death date: November 17, 1922

Age: 51

Marcel Proust was a French novelist, critic, and essayist whose monumental seven-volume work In Search of Lost Time transformed modern fiction through its exploration of memory, desire, art, society, and time. A brilliant observer of Parisian salons and inner life, he became one of the defining literary figures of the twentieth century. Long troubled by severe asthma and fragile health, he spent his final years increasingly confined while still revising his great novel. He died in Paris on 18 November 1922 from pneumonia and pulmonary complications at the age of 51.

Peter the Great, born Peter I Alekseyevich Romanov, was Tsar of Russia and later the first Emperor of Russia. He is remembered for transforming Russia into a major European power through military reform, naval expansion, administrative restructuring, Westernizing cultural policies, and the founding of Saint Petersburg. His reign reshaped the Russian state and left institutions that endured long after him. In his final years he suffered serious urinary and bladder illness; he died in Saint Petersburg on 8 February 1725 at the age of 52, with later accounts describing complications including uremia and gangrene of the bladder.

His writing explored absurdity, revolt, moral responsibility, and human dignity in a violent century. Camus died on 4 January 1960 at age 46 in a car crash near Sens, France, while traveling in a Facel Vega driven by his friend and publisher Michel Gallimard.

Enrico Fermi was an Italian-American physicist whose rare command of both theory and experiment helped shape modern nuclear and particle physics. He died in Chicago on 28 November 1954 from stomach cancer, aged 53, after an illness that cut short one of the most influential scientific careers of the twentieth century.

He became one of the 20th century’s most recognizable political icons, associated with anti-imperialism, guerrilla warfare, and revolutionary internationalism. After leaving Cuba to promote revolutions abroad, he fought in Bolivia, where he was captured by Bolivian forces and executed on 9 October 1967 at the age of 39.

Jane Austen was an English novelist whose sharply observant fiction transformed the novel of manners and helped shape literary realism. Best known for Pride and Prejudice, Sense and Sensibility, Emma, Mansfield Park, Persuasion, and Northanger Abbey, she wrote with wit, irony, and unusual insight into class, marriage, money, and women’s limited choices in Georgian society. Her fame grew greatly after her death, and her books have remained central to English literature. In her final year she suffered a serious, poorly understood illness, moved to Winchester to seek medical help, and died there on 18 July 1817 at the age of 41; later theories have included Addison’s disease, Hodgkin lymphoma, lupus, tuberculosis, and cancer.

Death date: August 18, 1662

Age: 39

Blaise Pascal was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher, and Catholic writer whose work shaped projective geometry, probability theory, fluid mechanics, and religious philosophy. A prodigy from childhood, he designed early calculating machines and later wrote the influential Lettres provinciales and Pensées. After years of fragile health, his illness worsened sharply in 1662; he suffered convulsions in Paris, received last rites, and died the next morning at age 39.

Kahlil Gibran was a Lebanese-American writer, poet, visual artist, and major figure of modern Arabic and English-language literature, best remembered for The Prophet, a 1923 work whose aphoristic spiritual prose reached readers around the world. Born in Bsharri and later active in Boston, Paris, and New York, he blended romanticism, mysticism, symbolism, and immigrant experience into a distinctive literary voice. He died in New York City on April 10, 1931, at age 48; contemporary accounts report cirrhosis of the liver, with incipient tuberculosis also noted.

John Calvin

Death date: May 26, 1564

Age: 54

John Calvin was a French theologian, pastor, lawyer, and one of the central figures of the Protestant Reformation. Based in Geneva, he shaped the Reformed tradition through his Institutes of the Christian Religion, biblical commentaries, and teachings on divine sovereignty and predestination. In his final years his health declined severely, including lung trouble and other chronic illnesses. He preached his last sermon in February 1564, said farewell to Geneva’s ministers in April, and died in Geneva on 27 May 1564 at the age of 54. He was buried in an unmarked grave to avoid turning his tomb into a shrine.

Michel Foucault was a French philosopher, historian of ideas, writer, critic, and teacher whose work reshaped modern thought about power, knowledge, institutions, sexuality, punishment, and social control. His major books include Madness and Civilization, The Order of Things, Discipline and Punish, and The History of Sexuality. He died in Paris on 25 June 1984 at the age of 57, after an illness widely described as AIDS-related, leaving later volumes of The History of Sexuality unfinished.

Age: 55

Claude Debussy was a French composer whose daring harmonies, fluid forms, and atmospheric orchestral color helped reshape modern music. Often linked with musical Impressionism, a label he disliked, he wrote landmark works such as Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune, Pelléas et Mélisande, La mer, and Clair de lune. He died in Paris of colon cancer on 25 March 1918, aged 55, while the city was under German bombardment during World War I, which made a large public funeral impossible.

Modern discussion of Gauguin often separates his artistic influence from serious criticism of his conduct and colonial context.

Paul Gauguin was a French Post-Impressionist painter, sculptor, printmaker, ceramist, and writer whose bold color, simplified forms, and Synthetist style helped move modern art beyond Impressionism. After years as a sailor and stockbroker, he devoted himself to art and became especially associated with Brittany, Tahiti, and the Marquesas. He died suddenly in Atuona on Hiva Oa in 1903, weakened by illness and pain; some accounts mention heart failure, morphine use, or other health complications. He was 54.

Born in Bohemia to a German-speaking Jewish family, he rose through major European opera posts and became director of the Vienna Court Opera before later working in New York. His final years were marked by heart trouble and serious infection; after a last conducting season in New York, he returned to Europe and died in Vienna on 18 May 1911 at age 50.

He worked on pioneering airmail routes across Europe, Africa and South America, and his books, including Night Flight, Wind, Sand and Stars and The Little Prince, combined adventure, moral reflection and poetic clarity. During World War II he flew reconnaissance missions for France. On 31 July 1944, aged 44, his aircraft disappeared over the Mediterranean during a mission near Corsica and Marseille; wreckage was later found, but the exact cause of the crash remains uncertain.

Dag Hammarskjöld was a Swedish economist, diplomat, and the second Secretary-General of the United Nations, serving from 1953 until 1961. He helped define the modern role of the UN chief through preventive diplomacy, peacekeeping, and a strong belief in an independent international civil service. His work during crises in the Middle East and Congo made him one of the most respected diplomats of the twentieth century. He died at age 56 when his aircraft crashed near Ndola, Northern Rhodesia, while he was traveling to negotiate a ceasefire during the Congo Crisis; the exact circumstances of the crash have remained the subject of later inquiries.

His only spaceflight made him one of the most celebrated figures of the 20th century. He died on 27 March 1968, aged 34, when the MiG-15UTI training aircraft he was flying with instructor Vladimir Seryogin crashed near Kirzhach; the exact cause remained disputed for decades.

Garfield was shot by Charles J. Guiteau on July 2, 1881, only months into his presidency, and died on September 19, 1881, after infections related to the wound.

His health failed in 1744; after receiving Catholic last rites, he died late at night at his Twickenham villa, surrounded by friends.

George VI, born Albert Frederick Arthur George, was King of the United Kingdom and the Dominions from 1936 to 1952. A reserved but dutiful monarch, he unexpectedly took the throne after the abdication of his brother Edward VIII and became a symbol of steadiness during the Second World War. He supported Britain through the Blitz, helped restore confidence in the monarchy, and was the father of Queen Elizabeth II. His later years were marked by serious smoking-related illness, including lung surgery; he died in his sleep at Sandringham on 6 February 1952, aged 56.

Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Highly controversial because he was a privateer involved in violent raids, imperial expansion, and early English slave-trading voyages. His reputation differs sharply between celebratory English naval history and perspectives that emphasize piracy, colonial violence, and slavery.

Sir Francis Drake was an English explorer, privateer, naval commander, and politician of the Elizabethan age, famed for completing the first English circumnavigation of the globe and for his role against the Spanish Armada. He was also involved in early English slaving voyages and became a feared raider of Spanish possessions. Drake died on 28 January 1596 during a failed expedition near Portobelo, Panama, most likely from dysentery, and was buried at sea in a lead-lined coffin.

Death date: November 10, 1855

Age: 42

Søren Aabye Kierkegaard was a Danish philosopher, theologian, poet, and religious writer whose probing works on faith, anxiety, choice, and individuality helped lay the foundations of existentialism. Writing both under his own name and under pseudonyms, he challenged abstract systems of thought and the complacency of official Christianity. In 1855, after an intense public attack on the Danish state church, he collapsed in Copenhagen and was taken to Frederiks Hospital. He remained there for over a month, refused communion from the official clergy, and died on 11 November 1855 at the age of 42.

After years of heavy smoking and declining health, he developed cancer around the esophagus. Surgery and treatment failed to stop the disease, and he died in Los Angeles on January 14, 1957, at age 57.

He died in Castres on 12 January 1665, apparently after illness, and epitaph-based research indicates he was 57 years old.

Restless and cosmopolitan, he lived and worked across Europe before spending his final years in Switzerland. Henry VIII was King of England from 1509 to 1547 and one of the defining rulers of the Tudor dynasty. Famous for his six marriages, his break with Rome, and the establishment of royal supremacy over the Church of England, he reshaped English politics, religion, and monarchy. In his final years he suffered severe physical decline, including obesity and a chronic ulcerated leg wound, and died at Whitehall Palace in London on 28 January 1547 at the age of 55.

Nicholas II, born Nikolai Alexandrovich Romanov, was the last Emperor of Russia, ruling from 1894 until his abdication during the upheaval of 1917. His reign saw industrial growth but also deep political unrest, the Russo-Japanese War, the 1905 Revolution, and the strains of World War I. After abdicating, he and his family were held by revolutionary authorities and were executed by Bolsheviks in Yekaterinburg on 17 July 1918, ending the Romanov dynasty’s rule.

Tycho Brahe was a Danish nobleman, astronomer, astrologer, and alchemist whose exceptionally precise pre-telescopic observations helped transform astronomy into a quantitative science. On the island of Hven he built Uraniborg and Stjerneborg, observatories that became centers of research, and his data later helped Johannes Kepler formulate the laws of planetary motion. He died in Prague on 24 October 1601, aged 54, after an acute bladder or kidney illness that followed a banquet; later studies found no convincing evidence that mercury poisoning killed him.

Robert Louis Stevenson was a Scottish novelist, poet, essayist and travel writer whose restless imagination produced Treasure Island, Kidnapped, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, and A Child's Garden of Verses. Born in Edinburgh and often weakened by chronic respiratory illness, he turned poor health and travel into literary energy, eventually settling in Samoa, where he became known as Tusitala, the teller of tales. On 3 December 1894, at his home in Vailima, he suddenly collapsed after speaking with his wife and died within hours, probably from a stroke or brain haemorrhage. Cleopatra VII Thea Philopator was the last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt and one of antiquity’s most politically skilled monarchs. A Greek-speaking queen from the Macedonian Ptolemaic dynasty, she ruled Egypt during the final crisis of the Roman Republic and allied herself first with Julius Caesar and later with Mark Antony. After Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra’s forces, Antony died by suicide, and Cleopatra followed shortly afterward in Alexandria, probably by poisoning, to avoid being displayed in a Roman triumph. John von Neumann

Birth date: December 27, 1903

Death date: February 7, 1957

Age: 53

John von Neumann was a Hungarian-American mathematician, physicist, computer scientist, and polymath whose work reshaped quantum mechanics, game theory, economics, functional analysis, nuclear strategy, and the architecture of modern computing. A brilliant and unusually versatile thinker, he worked at Princeton, the Institute for Advanced Study, Los Alamos, and the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission. In his final years he developed cancer, possibly linked by some accounts to wartime radiation exposure, and died at Walter Reed Army Medical Center in Washington, D.C., on February 8, 1957, at the age of 53.

Alphonse Daudet was a French novelist, short-story writer, playwright and poet, best remembered for Letters from My Mill, Tartarin of Tarascon and vivid portraits of provincial life in southern France. His health declined for years from a painful spinal illness linked to venereal disease, often identified as neurosyphilis or tabes dorsalis. Nikolai Gogol was a Ukrainian-born writer of the Russian Empire whose stories, plays, and novel Dead Souls reshaped Russian literature with satire, grotesque comedy, folklore, and psychological strangeness. Works such as The Nose, The Overcoat, The Government Inspector, and Taras Bulba made him a decisive influence on later writers from Dostoevsky to Kafka. In his final years he became increasingly religious, anxious, and physically weakened; after burning manuscripts, including material from the second part of Dead Souls, he refused food and died in Moscow at the age of 42.

Death date: April 30, 1945

Joseph Goebbels was a German Nazi politician, philologist, and one of Adolf Hitler’s closest associates, best known as the Reich Minister of Propaganda from 1933 to 1945. He shaped Nazi control of newspapers, radio, film, and public messaging, using propaganda to promote antisemitism, war mobilization, and loyalty to Hitler. In the final days of the Second World War, he remained in Berlin, briefly became Chancellor of Germany after Hitler’s suicide, and died by suicide with his wife Magda on 1 May 1945 after their six children had been poisoned.

Why this is controversial: Ivan the Terrible is highly controversial because his reign included extreme autocratic violence, the oprichnina, mass repression, executions, confiscations, and the massacre of Novgorod. His expansion and state-building are inseparable from severe brutality.

Ivan IV Vasilyevich, known as Ivan the Terrible, was Grand Prince of Moscow and the first Tsar of Russia, ruling during a dramatic transformation of Muscovy into a more centralized and expansionist state. His reign included legal and military reforms, the conquest of Kazan and Astrakhan, and the violent oprichnina that left a lasting mark on Russian history. He died in Moscow on 28 March 1584, traditionally said to have suffered a stroke while playing chess, leaving the throne to his son Feodor I.

Ferdinand de Saussure was a Swiss linguist, semiotician and philosopher whose ideas reshaped the study of language in the 20th century. He published little in his lifetime; his most famous work, Course in General Linguistics, was reconstructed from students' lecture notes and published after his death. Saussure died from cancer on 22 February 1913 at Vufflens-le-Château, Switzerland, aged 55, leaving much of his influence to grow posthumously.

Hermann Wilhelm Göring was a German politician, World War I fighter ace, military commander, and one of the most powerful figures in Nazi Germany. Mehmed II, known as Mehmed the Conqueror, was the Ottoman sultan whose capture of Constantinople in 1453 ended the Byzantine Empire and transformed the city into the empire’s great capital. A brilliant and ambitious ruler, he expanded Ottoman power across Anatolia and the Balkans while strengthening law, administration, architecture, and learning. In 1481, while setting out on another campaign, he became gravely ill near Gebze; gout was reported, and later accounts raised the possibility of poisoning. He died aged 49.

Pierre Curie was a French physicist and chemist whose work on crystallography, magnetism, piezoelectricity, and radioactivity helped shape modern physics. With Marie Curie and Henri Becquerel, he shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics for research on radiation. Robert Schumann was a German composer, pianist, and influential music critic of the early Romantic era, known for poetic piano works, songs, chamber music, symphonies, and his role in shaping Romantic musical thought through the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik. His marriage to pianist Clara Schumann became one of classical music’s most famous artistic partnerships. In his final years, Schumann’s mental and physical health declined severely; after a suicide attempt in 1854, he lived in a private sanatorium near Bonn and died there on 29 July 1856 at the age of 46.

Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Erwin Rommel is highly controversial because he was a senior commander in Nazi Germany's armed forces during World War II. His image has been shaped by propaganda and postwar mythmaking, including claims about his professionalism and distance from Nazi crimes, while historians continue to debate his relationship to the regime and his responsibility as an Axis commander.

Erwin Rommel was a German field marshal of World War II, best known as the “Desert Fox” for his command of Axis forces in North Africa and for his reputation as a bold armored-warfare tactician. His public image has remained contested, shaped by wartime propaganda, postwar mythmaking, and debate over his relationship to the Nazi regime. In October 1944, after being implicated in the aftermath of the 20 July plot against Hitler, he was forced to choose between trial and suicide; he died by cyanide poisoning at age 52.

Frank Vincent Zappa was an American composer, guitarist, songwriter, bandleader, filmmaker, satirist, and one of rock music’s great iconoclasts. His influential books include The Man in the High Castle, Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, Ubik, A Scanner Darkly, and VALIS, and many later became major films and television adaptations. In February 1982 he suffered a series of strokes, was hospitalized, and died in Santa Ana, California, on March 2, 1982, at the age of 53.

Heinrich Himmler was a German Nazi politician and military leader, best known as Reichsführer-SS and one of the most powerful figures in Nazi Germany. In the final weeks of World War II, after failed attempts to negotiate with the Western Allies, he was dismissed by Hitler, captured by British forces, and died by suicide in custody on 23 May 1945 at the age of 44.

Maximilien Robespierre was a French lawyer, Jacobin politician, and one of the most influential figures of the French Revolution. He championed political equality, universal male suffrage, civic virtue, and the abolition of the Atlantic slave trade, while becoming closely associated with the Committee of Public Safety and the Reign of Terror. In July 1794, amid rising fear of his power and policies, he was overthrown in the Thermidorian Reaction, arrested, and guillotined in Paris without trial at the age of 36.

He worked slowly, left a small surviving body of paintings, and also earned money as an art dealer. He died in Delft in December 1675 after a short illness, during years of economic strain that left his household burdened with debt.

After returning to Persia, he invested heavily in royal construction at Persepolis and Susa. Alexander III of Russia was Emperor of Russia, King of Poland, and Grand Duke of Finland from 1881 until 1894. A firm autocrat, he reversed many of Alexander II’s liberal reforms, promoted Russian nationalism, and became known as “the Peacemaker” because Russia fought no major wars during his reign. His later years were marked by declining health, and in 1894 he became gravely ill with kidney disease. Too weak to travel farther, he remained at Livadia in Crimea, where he died on 1 November 1894 at the age of 49.

Facing rebellion, abandonment by key supporters, and condemnation by the Senate, Nero fled Rome and died by suicide on 9 June AD 68 at the age of 30.

A brilliant, emotionally intense figure of 19th-century literature, he became associated with youthful passion, irony, disillusionment, and the artistic circles of Paris. He died in Paris in his sleep on 2 May 1857, aged 46; accounts commonly connect his final illness with heart failure, long-standing aortic insufficiency, and the effects of alcoholism.

Richard I of England, remembered as Richard the Lionheart, was a Plantagenet king famed for his military skill, leadership in the Third Crusade, and rule over a wide Angevin realm that included England, Normandy, Aquitaine, and Anjou. Controversies include the origins and truth claims of the Book of Mormon, plural marriage, theocratic power in Nauvoo, conflict with critics, destruction of an opposition press, and the enduring divide between believers' and critics' accounts of his life.

Joseph Smith Jr. was an American religious and political leader best known as the founder of Mormonism and the Latter Day Saint movement. He published the Book of Mormon in 1830 and organized a church that later developed into several denominations, including the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. His teachings, revelations, and leadership attracted many followers but also intense opposition. In 1844, after conflict in Nauvoo, Illinois, Smith was jailed in Carthage and was shot and killed by a mob at the age of 38.

Domitian

Birth date: October 23, 51

Death date: September 17, 96

Age: 44

Domitian, born Titus Flavius Domitianus, was Roman emperor from 81 to 96 CE and the last ruler of the Flavian dynasty. The son of Vespasian and younger brother of Titus, he strengthened imperial administration, promoted major building projects, and maintained strong support among the army and people, while alienating much of the Senate through authoritarian rule. He died at age 44 in Rome after being assassinated in a palace conspiracy by court officials, and was succeeded the same day by Nerva.

Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Titus is controversial because, before becoming emperor, he commanded Roman forces in the Jewish War and captured Jerusalem in 70 CE. That campaign involved mass death, enslavement, and the destruction of the Second Temple, one of the most traumatic events in Jewish history.

Titus Flavius Vespasianus was Roman emperor from 79 to 81 CE and a leading figure of the Flavian dynasty. Before ruling, he commanded Roman forces in the Jewish War and captured Jerusalem in 70, an event later commemorated by the Arch of Titus. As emperor he completed the Colosseum and became known for disaster relief after Vesuvius and a major fire in Rome. His reign was brief: after the amphitheatre games, he fell ill and died of fever on 13 September 81, aged 41, and was succeeded by his brother Domitian.

Guillaume Apollinaire was a Polish-French poet, playwright, novelist, journalist, and art critic who helped shape the avant-garde culture of early twentieth-century Paris. During World War I he served in the French army and suffered a serious head wound in 1916. Weakened by that injury, he died in Paris during the 1918 influenza pandemic, just two days before the Armistice, at the age of 38.

Louis XII of France, born Louis of Orléans, ruled France from 1498 to 1515 and was also briefly King of Naples. Remembered as the “Father of the People” for tax reductions, legal reforms, and relative domestic calm, he also pursued costly Italian campaigns and strengthened the link between Brittany and France through his marriage to Anne of Brittany. In his final months he married Mary Tudor in a last attempt to secure a male heir, but he was already in declining health. After a severe attack of gout around Christmas 1514, he received the final sacraments on 1 January 1515 and died that evening in Paris at age 52, leaving the throne to Francis I.

Why this is controversial: Shaka Zulu is controversial because his state-building and military reforms are associated with conquest, harsh discipline, executions, and regional upheaval. At the same time, many accounts of his brutality were shaped by hostile or colonial-era sources, so the historical picture is debated.

Shaka kaSenzangakhona, widely known as Shaka Zulu, was the powerful founder and king of the Zulu Kingdom, remembered for reshaping military organization, discipline, and regional politics in southern Africa. His reign from about 1816 to 1828 helped turn the Zulu from a smaller chiefdom into a major force. He was assassinated at KwaDukuza by his half-brothers Dingane and Mhlangana, with Mbopa also traditionally named among the conspirators, after mounting tensions in the royal court.

Dzhokhar Dudayev was a Chechen military officer, politician, and former Soviet Air Force major general who became the first president of the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria in 1991. Catherine of Aragon was a Spanish princess, daughter of Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile, and became Queen of England as the first wife of Henry VIII. After Henry sought an annulment and broke with papal authority, Catherine was removed from court and recognized only as Dowager Princess of Wales. She spent her final years at Kimbolton Castle, where she died on 7 January 1536, probably from cancer, at the age of 50.

Eva Perón, widely known as Evita, was an Argentine actress, political leader, and First Lady of Argentina from 1946 to 1952 as the wife of President Juan Perón. She became a central figure of Peronism, championed labor rights and women's suffrage, founded the Female Peronist Party, and led the Eva Perón Foundation, which made her beloved among many working-class Argentines. In 1951, declining health and opposition from powerful institutions forced her to abandon a bid for the vice presidency. She died of cancer in Buenos Aires on 1952-07-26 at the age of 33 and received a state funeral.

Death date: May 13, 1643

Louis XIII of France, known as Louis the Just, became king as a child after the assassination of his father Henry IV and ruled during a decisive stage in the rise of Bourbon power. Working closely with Cardinal Richelieu, he helped strengthen royal authority, confront noble rebellions and the Huguenots, and position France against Habsburg Spain. His reign also saw the birth of the future Louis XIV. After a long final illness, probably involving tuberculosis and severe intestinal disease, Louis XIII died on 14 May 1643 at the age of 41.

Plath’s writing turned personal anguish into disciplined art, exploring identity, ambition, motherhood, alienation, and self-destruction with rare force. She died by suicide in London on February 11, 1963, during a severe depressive period, at the age of 30.

Christian Andreas Doppler was an Austrian mathematician and physicist whose name became attached to one of the most familiar ideas in wave science: the Doppler effect, the change in observed frequency caused by motion between source and observer. His final years were marked by worsening chest and lung problems, probably tuberculosis; seeking a gentler climate, he went to Venice, where he died on 1853-03-17 at age 49.

His legacy helped inspire later Zapatismo and made him an enduring symbol of social justice in Mexico. Zapata died at age 39 on 10 April 1919, when he was lured into an ambush at Chinameca, Morelos, and assassinated by forces linked to Venustiano Carranza.

Death date: February 19, 1790

Age: 48

Joseph II was Holy Roman Emperor from 1765 and sole ruler of the Habsburg Monarchy from 1780, remembered as one of Europe’s most energetic enlightened absolutists. He pushed reforms in religion, law, education, administration, serfdom, and state centralization, often faster than his empire could absorb. His final years were clouded by war, resistance in Hungary and the Austrian Netherlands, and the rollback of several reforms. Already seriously ill after returning to Vienna, he suffered worsening fever, coughing, breathing problems, and chest pain, probably linked to pulmonary tuberculosis, and died in Vienna at age 48.

Nicknamed “Iron Felix,” he became one of the most feared and symbolic figures of early Soviet power, closely associated with the Red Terror and the creation of a repressive security apparatus. He died in Moscow on 20 July 1926 after suffering a heart attack, reportedly shortly after delivering a forceful speech to the Bolshevik Central Committee.

Ryūnosuke Akutagawa

Death date: July 23, 1927

Age: 35

Ryūnosuke Akutagawa was a Japanese writer of the Taishō period, celebrated for sharply crafted short stories such as Rashōmon, In a Grove, The Nose, and Hell Screen. Often called a defining figure of the modern Japanese short story, he gave his name to Japan’s prestigious Akutagawa Prize. In his final years he struggled with anxiety, fragile health, and fear of mental illness; on 24 July 1927, he died by suicide from a barbital overdose in Tokyo at the age of 35.

Simone Weil

Birth date: February 2, 1909

Death date: August 23, 1943

Age: 34

Simone Weil was a French philosopher, mystic, teacher, writer, and political activist whose short life left a lasting mark on political thought, religious philosophy, and ethics. Born in Paris to a secular Jewish family, she taught, supported labor movements, worked in factories to understand working-class life, and briefly joined anti-fascist forces during the Spanish Civil War. During World War II she worked with the Free French in Britain. Already weakened by illness, tuberculosis, and severe self-denial, she died in Ashford, Kent, from cardiac failure linked to poor health and restricted eating, aged 34.

Christopher Marlowe, also known as Kit Marlowe, was one of the defining voices of Elizabethan drama: a playwright, poet, translator, and major predecessor of Shakespeare. His life ended abruptly in Deptford in 1593, when he was stabbed during a disputed altercation involving Ingram Frizer; the official account called it self-defence, though the circumstances have remained famously controversial.

Death date: June 14, 1889

Age: 39

Mihai Eminescu was Romania’s great Romantic poet, novelist, and journalist, celebrated for giving Romanian literature some of its most enduring works, including Luceafărul and the Letters. A member of the Junimea circle and an editor at Timpul, he became a national literary symbol through poetry rich in myth, history, love, nature, and metaphysical reflection. His final years were marked by severe illness, psychiatric confinement, and controversial medical treatment. He died in Bucharest on 15 June 1889, aged 39, in a sanatorium, with the precise medical cause still debated.

Death date: March 3, 1832

Age: 41

Jean-François Champollion was a French philologist and orientalist best known for deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs, a breakthrough that opened ancient Egyptian texts to modern scholarship and made him a founding figure of Egyptology. A gifted linguist from youth, he used Coptic, Greek, and the Rosetta Stone to show that hieroglyphs combined phonetic and ideographic signs. After a demanding scholarly career and an expedition to Egypt, his health deteriorated; he died in Paris on 4 March 1832, reportedly after an apoplectic attack, at the age of 41.

Sándor Petőfi was a Hungarian poet, journalist and revolutionary, widely regarded as Hungary's national poet and one of the defining voices of the 1848 Revolution. He disappeared during the Battle of Segesvár on 31 July 1849 while serving with the revolutionary forces; he is generally believed to have been killed there, although his body was never conclusively identified.

Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Georges Danton was a major figure of the French Revolution and is closely associated with revolutionary violence, the fall of the monarchy, and the political climate that led into the Reign of Terror. He was also accused by opponents of corruption and betrayal, though those accusations were politically charged.

Georges Jacques Danton was one of the most powerful voices of the French Revolution: a lawyer, electrifying orator, Cordeliers Club figure, minister of justice, and early member of the Committee of Public Safety. He helped shape the fall of the monarchy and the rise of the First French Republic, but later called for moderation during the Terror. Accused of corruption, conspiracy, and political betrayal by his enemies, he was tried by the Revolutionary Tribunal and guillotined in Paris on 5 April 1794 at the age of 34.

Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Eva Braun is highly controversial because she was Adolf Hitler's longtime companion and briefly his wife, lived inside his private circle during the Nazi dictatorship, and is strongly associated with the leadership environment of a regime responsible for genocide, aggressive war, and mass persecution.

Eva Braun was a German photographer and the longtime companion of Adolf Hitler, whom she met while working for Heinrich Hoffmann, Hitler’s photographer. For years she lived largely out of public view, becoming part of Hitler’s private circle at the Berghof and leaving behind many photographs and films of that world. In the final days of Nazi Germany, she joined Hitler in the Berlin Führerbunker, married him on 29 April 1945, and died by suicide with cyanide the next day as Soviet troops closed in.

José Rizal was a Filipino nationalist, novelist, physician, and reformist thinker whose writings, especially Noli Me Tangere and El filibusterismo, helped expose abuses under Spanish colonial rule and inspired the Philippine nationalist movement. After the Philippine Revolution began, Spanish authorities accused him of rebellion; he was tried by court-martial and executed by firing squad at Bagumbayan, Manila, on 30 December 1896, at age 35, becoming a powerful martyr figure in Philippine history.

Martin Ludwig Bormann was a German Nazi Party official who became one of Adolf Hitler’s most powerful aides, serving as head of the Nazi Party Chancellery and Hitler’s private secretary. He controlled access to Hitler, influenced appointments and legislation, and was later convicted in absentia at the Nuremberg trials for war crimes and crimes against humanity. As Soviet forces closed in on Berlin, Bormann fled the Führerbunker on 2 May 1945 and most likely died by suicide near Lehrter station; his remains were found decades later and confirmed as his.

Spartacus

Birth date: December 31, 103 BCE

Death date: March 31, 71 BCE

Age: 32

Spartacus was a Thracian gladiator who became the most famous leader of the Third Servile War, the major slave uprising against the Roman Republic from 73 to 71 BC. After escaping a gladiatorial school near Capua, he helped turn a small band of fugitives into a powerful rebel force that defeated several Roman armies. His life is known mostly from later writers such as Plutarch and Appian, and he became an enduring symbol of resistance against oppression. In 71 BC, his army was finally defeated by forces under Marcus Licinius Crassus; Spartacus is believed to have been killed in the final battle, though his body was never identified.

Carl Wilhelm Scheele

Birth date: December 8, 1742

Death date: May 20, 1786

Age: 43

Carl Wilhelm Scheele was a German-Swedish pharmaceutical chemist whose experimental skill made him one of the most productive chemical discoverers of the eighteenth century. He independently discovered oxygen before Joseph Priestley published, identified chlorine, and helped reveal substances connected with molybdenum, tungsten, barium, manganese, and many organic and inorganic acids. He worked mainly as a pharmacist rather than as a university professor, which partly explains why his fame lagged behind his achievements. Scheele died in Köping on 21 May 1786 at the age of 43, after years of dangerous laboratory exposure; contemporary and later accounts often connect his decline with poisoning from toxic substances such as mercury, arsenic, lead compounds, cyanides, and acids.

Gavrilo Princip was a Bosnian Serb student and South Slav nationalist best known for assassinating Archduke Franz Ferdinand and Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914, an act that helped set off World War I. Carl Maria von Weber was a German composer, conductor, virtuoso pianist, guitarist, and critic whose operas helped define German Romantic opera. Works such as Der Freischütz, Euryanthe, and Oberon influenced later composers including Wagner, while his clarinet and piano music remained important in the concert repertoire. In 1826, already weakened by tuberculosis, he travelled to London to finish and conduct Oberon. After the premiere and a demanding run of performances, his health collapsed; he died in his sleep at the home of Sir George Smart on 5 June 1826, aged 39.

Brother of Edward IV, he became king after the young Edward V and his brother were declared illegitimate, a controversy tied forever to the mystery of the Princes in the Tower. Peter III of Russia, born Karl Peter Ulrich of Schleswig-Holstein-Gottorp, was the grandson of Peter the Great and briefly ruled as Emperor of Russia in 1762. His short reign brought reforms, but his admiration for Prussia and reversal of Russian gains in the Seven Years’ War made him deeply unpopular among powerful elites. After only about six months on the throne, he was overthrown in a palace coup led by supporters of his wife, Catherine II. He was taken to Ropsha and died soon afterward under murky circumstances, officially explained as illness but widely suspected to have involved violence.

Caracalla, born Lucius Septimius Bassianus and later known as Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, was a Severan Roman emperor and the son of Septimius Severus and Julia Domna. He ruled first alongside his father, briefly with his brother Geta, and then alone after Geta’s murder. His reign is remembered for the Antonine Constitution, which extended Roman citizenship to most free inhabitants of the empire, and for the monumental Baths of Caracalla in Rome. In 217, while campaigning in the East against Parthia, he was assassinated near Carrhae by a soldier, Justin Martialis, in a plot associated with the future emperor Macrinus.

As head of the Reich Security Main Office, he oversaw major instruments of Nazi terror, including the Gestapo, Kripo, and SD, and chaired the 1942 Wannsee Conference, where plans for the genocide of Europe’s Jews were coordinated. He was mortally wounded in Prague during Operation Anthropoid, an assassination carried out by Czechoslovak agents, and died of sepsis from his injuries on 4 June 1942 at the age of 38.

Catherine of Siena was an Italian mystic, Dominican tertiary, writer, and political-religious mediator whose letters and spiritual works made her one of the most influential women of medieval Catholicism. She died in Rome on 29 April 1380 at age 33, weakened by severe fasting and illness; traditions and modern summaries often connect her final decline with a paralytic stroke shortly before death.

Edward IV of England

Birth date: April 27, 1442

Death date: April 8, 1483

Age: 40

Edward IV was the first Yorkist king of England and one of the central rulers of the Wars of the Roses. He seized the throne from Henry VI in 1461, lost it briefly in 1470, and regained it after decisive victories at Barnet and Tewkesbury in 1471. His later reign was comparatively stable, though shaped by dynastic tension and the political consequences of his marriage to Elizabeth Woodville. He fell seriously ill around Easter 1483 and died at Westminster on 9 April 1483, aged 40; his young son Edward V succeeded him but was soon displaced by Richard III.

Domenico Ghirlandaio was a leading Florentine Renaissance painter, famous for lively narrative frescoes, portraits of contemporary Florentines, and a large workshop that trained artists including Michelangelo. He died in Florence on 11 January 1494, aged 45, reportedly during an outbreak of plague or pestilential fever, and was buried in Santa Maria Novella.

Age: 36

Charles XII of Sweden, also known as Karl XII or Carolus Rex, was the Swedish king from 1697 to 1718 and one of the most famous warrior-monarchs of the Great Northern War. He inherited the throne as a teenager, defeated major enemies early in his reign, and became closely associated with Sweden’s last great-power era. His Russian campaign ended disastrously after Poltava, weakening the Swedish Empire. He died aged 36 during the siege of Fredriksten in Norway, when a projectile struck him in the head; modern research suggests enemy-fired iron grapeshot was the likely cause.

Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg was a German army officer and aristocrat who became one of the most important figures in the military resistance to Nazism. On 20 July 1944, he placed a bomb at Hitler’s Wolf’s Lair headquarters as part of Operation Valkyrie. The assassination failed, and Stauffenberg was arrested and executed in Berlin shortly after midnight, dying at the age of 36.

Charles V of France, known as Charles the Wise, ruled from 1364 to 1380 and became one of the most effective Valois kings during the Hundred Years’ War. With careful taxation, diplomacy, fortified cities, a reorganized army, and commanders such as Bertrand du Guesclin, he recovered much of the territory lost to England and strengthened royal government. In his final years he suffered from a long-standing abscess or fistula; when it dried up in September 1380, he prepared for death, tried to abolish the unpopular hearth tax, and died at 42, leaving the throne to his young son Charles VI.

Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Guy Fawkes was part of the Gunpowder Plot, a conspiracy to blow up Parliament and kill King James I. He is remembered both as a symbol of resistance and as a participant in an attempted mass-casualty political assassination.

Guy Fawkes, also known as Guido Fawkes, was an English soldier and Catholic conspirator best remembered for his role in the Gunpowder Plot of 1605, a failed attempt to blow up the House of Lords and kill King James I. Born in York, he fought for Catholic Spain before joining Robert Catesby's conspiracy. After being discovered guarding barrels of gunpowder beneath Parliament, he was tortured, tried for high treason, and sentenced to be hanged, drawn and quartered. On 31 January 1606, he died at the gallows in Westminster, reportedly breaking his neck and avoiding the full brutality of the sentence.

Elagabalus was a teenage Roman emperor of the Severan dynasty who ruled from 218 to 222 CE after rising from his role as priest of the sun god Elagabal in Emesa. His reign became famous for religious upheaval, court scandal, and conflict with Rome’s political elite; in March 222 he was assassinated by the Praetorian Guard during a coup and replaced by Severus Alexander.

Katherine Mansfield, born Kathleen Mansfield Beauchamp in Wellington, New Zealand, was one of the defining short-story writers of literary modernism. Her sharp, lyrical fiction explored memory, identity, intimacy, social performance, and the tensions of colonial and European life. She built a lasting reputation in England and Europe and was connected to major modernist circles around writers such as Virginia Woolf and D. H. Lawrence. Mansfield’s health collapsed after she developed tuberculosis, diagnosed in 1917. She spent her final years moving through Europe in search of relief and unconventional treatments, and died in France near Fontainebleau on 9 January 1923 at the age of 34.

Charles IX of France

Birth date: June 26, 1550

Death date: May 29, 1574

Age: 23
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Charles IX of France is highly controversial because his reign is closely associated with the French Wars of Religion and the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre, in which thousands of Huguenots were killed. Historians debate the exact degree of his personal responsibility, but his name remains tied to one of France's most notorious episodes of religious violence.

Charles IX of France was King of France from 1560 to 1574, a Valois monarch whose reign was dominated by the French Wars of Religion and the struggle between Catholics and Huguenots. He is best known for his connection to the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre in 1572, one of the most notorious episodes in French history. In his final years his health and state of mind declined, and he died of tuberculosis at Vincennes in 1574 at the age of 23.

Osman II, better known as Genç Osman or Osman the Young, was the reform-minded 16th sultan of the Ottoman Empire, ruling from 1618 to 1622. Intelligent and ambitious, he tried to strengthen central authority after the failed campaign against Poland and challenged the power of the Janissaries, moves that made him one of the most dramatic young rulers in Ottoman history. In May 1622, after a military revolt in Constantinople, he was deposed, taken to Yedikule Fortress, and strangled.

Valentinian III

Birth date: July 1, 419

Death date: March 15, 455

Age: 35

Valentinian III was Western Roman emperor from 425 to 455, placed on the throne as a child and long overshadowed by his mother Galla Placidia and the general Flavius Aetius. His reign saw the Western Empire weakened by internal power struggles, Vandal expansion in North Africa, and pressure from the Huns under Attila. In 454 Valentinian personally killed Aetius after falling under suspicion and court intrigue. The next year, on 16 March 455, he was assassinated in Rome by former followers of Aetius, a violent end that further destabilized the already collapsing western imperial government.

Maximilian I of Mexico was an Austrian archduke of the House of Habsburg-Lorraine and the younger brother of Emperor Franz Joseph I. After service in the Austrian Navy and as viceroy of Lombardy-Venetia, he accepted the Mexican crown in 1864 with French backing and became emperor of the Second Mexican Empire. His liberal-leaning policies alienated many conservative supporters, while republican forces under Benito Juárez continued to resist. After French troops withdrew, Maximilian was captured at Querétaro, tried by the restored republic, and executed by firing squad on 19 June 1867 at the age of 34.

Blackbeard

Birth date: December 31, 1680

Death date: November 21, 1718

Age: 38
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Blackbeard is highly controversial because he was a pirate whose fame rests on maritime robbery, intimidation, hostage-taking, and violence. Later popular culture often romanticizes him, but his historical reputation is tied to criminal raiding and fear.

Blackbeard, born Edward Teach or Thatch, was an English pirate whose short but spectacular career made him the model of the terrifying sea raider. Operating in the West Indies and along the North American coast, he captured La Concorde, renamed it Queen Anne's Revenge, and built his reputation through intimidation, theatrical menace, and daring attacks such as the blockade of Charles Town. After accepting a pardon and returning to piracy, he was cornered near Ocracoke by a force led by Lieutenant Robert Maynard. On 22 November 1718, Blackbeard was killed in a violent boarding fight, reportedly suffering multiple gunshot and blade wounds before being beheaded.

Did you know:

For most of history, a drink of water was also a gamble. Rivers, wells, and town pumps could carry sewage-borne diseases such as cholera and typhoid. In the United States, typhoid fever was about 100 cases per 100,000 people in 1900; after water treatment, sanitation, and disinfection spread, it fell to 33.8 by 1920 and 0.1 by 2006. A glass of boring tap water may be one of the greatest inventions in history.

The humbling part is that this is not ancient history everywhere. WHO estimates that around 1 million people still die each year from diarrhoea linked to unsafe drinking water, sanitation, and hand hygiene. So when someone in a modern city turns a tap, showers, brushes teeth, and flushes a toilet without thinking, they are living inside a public-health miracle.
